<reason>CON chose the cleanest possible route against a universal claim — find one justified bounded pause — and executed it with discipline, correctly insisting that timing matters and that PRO cannot call mandatory review enforceable while calling mandatory restoration fictional. But PRO landed two damaging structural hits that CON never fully dislodged. First, PRO showed CON's opening example was mis-specified: an account-takeover hold treats the claimant as victim, not suspect, forcing CON to rebuild the scenario mid-debate. Second, and decisively, PRO read the motion as it is written — "solely... without meaningful human review" — and pointed out that every version of CON's exception bundles in notice, reasons, an urgent hardship channel, prompt human reconsideration, and default restoration. CON therefore never actually defended a suspension unaccompanied by meaningful human review; it defended a suspension without *prior* review, which is a narrower and arguably compliant thing. CON asserted that timing is dispositive but never grounded that reading of the text against PRO's duration-based reading. PRO's closing dilemma — the safeguards CON requires are themselves capacity commitments, so the exception is safe where it is unnecessary and necessary where it is unsafe — sharpened rather than merely recapped, and CON's symmetry reply, though good, only partially blunted it. PRO also held the harm-asymmetry point (recoverable overpayment vs irreversible eviction), which CON answered in a single line. PRO's use of the Dutch childcare, Robodebt and Michigan cases was general, plausible, and free of brittle precision. PRO carries an execution cost for two clipped, over-length turns, which is why the margin stays modest rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's turn of CON's own safeguards against it: because CON's exception guarantees expiry, notice, hardship access and prompt human reconsideration with default restoration, CON was haggling over minutes rather than defending a deprivation that stands on a score alone — and CON's later "timing is decisive" reply asserted, rather than established, that the motion requires review *before* rather than simply *at all*.</best_rebuttal>
